**Yes.** There is enough bare tabletop behind the solid white kettle to take the floral
teapot, and it would sit there without touching or overhanging the far edge of the table.

behind it.

## Which objects I mean

- **Solid white kettle** — the tall, plain cream/white coffee pot with the straight spout
  and the loop handle, at the back left of the photo.
- **Floral kettle** — the squat, round teapot on the right in the second row, painted with

### 1. The far edge of the table is visible, and there is clear wood behind the white kettle

Right across the top of the picture there is a crisp horizontal line where the dark
polished wood stops and the background begins — the slatted chair backs and the cream wall
sit above that line and are cut off by it. That line is the far edge of the table. It runs

The white kettle's base sits well forward of that line. Between the back of its base and
the table's far edge there is an unbroken band of empty, unoccupied tabletop — nothing is
standing in it. So the question is only whether that band is deep enough.

### 2. The band is deeper than it looks, because perspective compresses distance

This is the key point, and it is also the main trap in the picture. Two things make the
strip *look* smaller than it is:

- The white kettle is **tall**, so its lid and finial rise up past the table‑edge line in
  the image. That is the kettle's height, not its position: it looks as if the pot is
  jammed against the edge when in fact its foot is a long way forward of it.
- Depth in the back of a photograph is squashed. A centimetre of table near the far edge
  occupies far fewer pixels than a centimetre of table in the foreground, so the empty
  strip reads as a thin ribbon even though it is a broad expanse of wood.

### 3. Measuring it against a known object — the saucers

The gold‑rimmed saucers are all the same and are about 15–16 cm across, so they make a

### 4. How much room the floral kettle actually needs
